doc.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Fighting record companies to let Joe Williams sing ballads
summary: Joe was billed as jazz and blues despite his ballad ability; Levy fought for strings and 'Here's to Life', quit Polygram, and finally did it with Telarc.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: When you started with Joe, as far as his place in the marketplace for records, was he billed as strictly as jazz singer? Was he a, you know, a blues singer? What was his—

Yeah. He was booked as a jazz and blues, and that was it. And nobody realized or knew, his ability to sing, except people in Chicago who knew him years before. Because Joe used to sing in a night club where you didn’t even see him. The girls walked out and —

Yeah. All you could hear was his voice, and you know, he’d sing like “A Pretty Girl Is Like a Melody,” and these girls would walk around. And you never saw him. And he’d go on the air, like I think he was with Jimmy Noone. And he’d go on the air and sing nothing but ballads you know, just nothing but pretty tunes. But nobody paid any attention to that. A recording company didn’t want to know about that. They didn’t want to record Joe doing any ballads or anything. Right up until the last few years, we had to fight in order to really get them to allow Joe to sing a ballad. “Here’s to Life” we had that tune for years before Shirley Horn recorded it and we’d been trying to get to record it and they would not, nobody wants it, “no, that’s not Joe.” You know, “that’s not Joe.” You know it’s a pretty tune and all that. And I insisted on a full orchestra, too, that’s the next thing. And nobody wanted to come up with that full orchestra. “Oh it costs too much, you know, why don’t Joe just sing the blues and get a little group together and that’s it.” And I had to fight. And in fact I quit Polygram for that reason, just walked out, said forget it, you know. Are we going to do this? This is the next project or no project at all. That was it. And finally Telarc agreed to do it. And but we still had to do a Basie album with Basie first. And then we got the deal to go to London and got Quantum to do the Telarc, the full strings and everything, the album that we wanted to do and had been fighting to do for years. The next thing we had been trying to do over the years was a spiritual album. He finally got that off of Telarc. So it’s been a good thing with them because they’ve allowed him to do what he wanted to do for years and couldn’t get on. We’d been trying, you know, every record company he’s been with, he had been trying to do these things.

Because when he started out, actually RCA Victor did do some really beautiful things with big bands and strings and things. They never did anything with the records, but you know, this was the era of “A Man Ain’t Supposed To Cry” I think, and some of those things that they did in those days. But they never did anything with them. Because they were pretty ballad things, and they didn’t know how to promote them, they just satisfied Joe, you know.

That’s funny, because you know you read about the rock ‘N roll bands, and they have the same problems you know. They’re dissatisfied with their record companies because, you know, “well we’ve done these albums for you now we want to do this new type of thing.” And the record company says, “no, stay with this sound.”
Yeah. They want to stay with the tried and true, what they can sell easily.
I wonder if they do that with classical musicians. “Don’t record any Schubert, stick with the Mozart.”
